corpus_definition: a range of different types of things

forms.definition: a number of different types of things in one group
forms.example: The market in Chorsu has a wide variety of spices.

syn.note: Very close: 'a wide range of fruit'. Common in shops and adverts.
A group of things you can choose from, often in a shop.
Easy word: 'a big choice of drinks' means many different drinks.
More formal; often about people, cultures or nature.
Different things together, but not always many types.

forms.definition: a change or difference in amount or level
forms.example: There is a big variation in prices between the two shops.

forms.definition: to be different from each other in size, amount or type
forms.example: Prices vary from shop to shop.
forms.note: Variety is made from this verb.

syn.note: Very close, a little more formal.
Vary often means 'be different in different places or times', not just 'become different'.

forms.definition: of several different types or kinds
forms.example: We visited various cities in Uzbekistan last summer.

syn.note: Easy word; 'different' can also mean 'not the same', but various only means 'several types'.
Several is about number; various is about different types.
More formal: very different from each other.

forms.definition: including many different types of things
forms.example: She has a very varied diet with lots of vegetables.

forms.definition: often changing and not staying the same
forms.example: The weather in spring is very variable.
forms.note: Belongs to vary = change often, not a range of different types.

forms.definition: in several different ways
forms.example: The tower has been variously described as beautiful and ugly.

syn.note: In a way that is not the same.

people.definition: a form of something that is a little different from others
people.example: This is a new variant of the virus.

context.text: Our school canteen now offers a wide variety of dishes. The menu varies every day, and you can choose from various salads and soups.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows share one meaning (range of types), merged at A2. variable kept as other_meaning (vary = change).

corpus_definition: a decorative container used for holding flowers or water

forms.definition: a pretty container that you put flowers in
forms.example: She put the roses in a tall glass vase.

syn.note: A pot is usually for plants with soil; a vase holds cut flowers in water.
A jar is for food like jam or honey, but people sometimes put flowers in one.
General word for anything that holds something.

context.text: For Women's Day, Aziz bought his mother some tulips. She put them in her blue vase on the kitchen table.

reviewer_note: No other family forms exist; pronunciation difference noted.

corpus_definition: A long-distance chat where you can see the other person.
usage_note: have / make a video call (with someone): 'We had a video call with Grandma.' Also used as a verb in informal English: 'I'll video call you tonight.'

relations.note: Same meaning, a little more informal.
You talk, but usually you cannot see the other person.
A call on an app with sound only, no video.

context.text: My brother works in Seoul, so we have a video call every Sunday. My little sister loves the video call because she can show him her drawings.

reviewer_note: Compound noun, kind phrase; informal verb use noted.

corpus_definition: A digital game played on a computer or television screen.
usage_note: play a video game / play video games: 'He plays video games after school.' Often plural when talking about the hobby.

relations.note: Almost the same; computer game is more common in British English.
General word: games can also be board games or sports.
A game played on a table with a board, not on a screen.

context.text: Timur plays video games for an hour after his homework. His favourite video game is about football.

corpus_definition: Someone who goes to see a person or a place.

forms.definition: a person who goes to see a person or a place
forms.example: Samarkand gets thousands of visitors every summer.

syn.note: A person you invite to your home or a hotel customer.
A person who travels for fun to see places.
A person who comes to your house for a short time; a bit old-fashioned.

ant.note: The person who welcomes guests at home.

forms.definition: an occasion when you go to see a person or place
forms.example: Our visit to Bukhara was short but fun.

syn.note: A trip is the journey; a visit is the time you spend there.

forms.definition: to go to see a person or a place
forms.example: We visit my grandparents every weekend.

syn.note: Easy phrase with the same meaning.
Visit a person for a short time; a bit formal.
Visit for a short time without planning.
Easy word: 'I saw my aunt yesterday.'

forms.definition: coming to a place for a short time, often to work or play
forms.example: The visiting team won the match 2-1.

syn.note: In sport, the visiting team is the away team.

ant.note: In sport, the home team plays in its own city.

context.text: Many visitors come to Khiva in spring. When you visit the old city, you can climb the tall minaret and see the walls.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun, so it stays main in the noun slot (rule 6); visit noun added as extra.

corpus_definition: to choose your leader or preference in an election.

forms.definition: a choice that a person makes in an election
forms.example: Every vote is important in this election.

syn.note: Formal: the paper or system used to choose.
General word for what you choose.

forms.definition: the act of choosing someone or something in an election
forms.example: Voting starts at eight in the morning.

forms.definition: to show your choice in an election
forms.example: My parents vote in every election.

syn.note: Elect = choose a person for a job by voting; you elect a person, but you vote for a person.
Easy general word; vote is choosing in an official way.
Formal phrase used in news.

ant.note: Formal: to choose not to vote.

people.definition: a person who chooses someone in an election

context.text: Next week our class will vote for a new class leader. Voting starts after lunch, and each student has one vote.

reviewer_note: vote verb and noun share spelling (conversion); voter is a person, so it is in People.

corpus_definition: a vehicle with four wheels pulled by a horse

forms.definition: a vehicle with four wheels that a horse pulls, used for carrying things
forms.example: The farmer loaded hay onto the wooden wagon.
forms.note: Old British spelling: waggon. In British English it can also mean a train car for goods.

syn.note: Often smaller, sometimes with two wheels.
A carriage pulled by horses carries people, not goods.

context.text: In the village, my grandfather still has an old wagon. Every autumn he puts melons in it and his horse pulls it to the market.

reviewer_note: No other family forms; spelling and train-car meaning noted.

corpus_definition: A large piece of furniture used for hanging up clothes.

forms.definition: a tall cupboard where you hang your clothes
forms.example: She hung her new dress in the wardrobe.
forms.note: It can also mean all the clothes a person has: 'a new summer wardrobe'.

syn.note: American English; often built into the wall.
General word for furniture with doors and shelves, often in the kitchen.

context.text: My room is small, but it has a big wardrobe. All my shirts and my winter coat are in the wardrobe.

reviewer_note: No other family forms; second meaning (all your clothes) noted.

corpus_definition: to clean the plates, cups, and cutlery used for eating
particle_note: Usually without an object: 'I'll wash up.' With an object it is separable: 'wash up the cups / wash the cups up'. British English; in American English wash up means 'wash your hands and face'. Noun: the washing-up.

relations.note: Same meaning, common in American and British English.
British English, very common at home.
General word; you can clean anything, not just plates.

context.text: After dinner, my mother cooks tea and I wash up. Tonight my brother washed the plates up because it was my birthday.

reviewer_note: British vs American meaning difference noted.

corpus_definition: to use something in a bad way so it is gone

forms.definition: using money, time or things in a bad or careless way
forms.example: Buying that phone was a waste of money.

syn.note: Using something in the wrong way, not only too much.
Something you no longer have; not always your fault.

ant.note: Keeping money, time or things instead of using them.

forms.definition: to use money, time or things badly so that they are gone
forms.example: Don't waste your time playing games all day.

syn.note: Formal: waste something valuable, like money or a chance.
Informal: 'He threw away his chance.'
Use all of something; not always in a bad way.

ant.note: Keep money, time or things for later.
Formal: use water or energy carefully.

forms.definition: using more money, time or things than you need
forms.example: Leaving the lights on all night is wasteful.

syn.note: Spending a lot of money, often on things you do not need.
Not thinking about what you do.

ant.note: Not using much money, fuel or time.

forms.definition: not useful because it gave no result
forms.example: It was a wasted trip; the shop was closed.

forms.definition: in a way that uses more than you need
forms.example: Some hotels use water very wastefully.

syn.note: Spending a lot of money.

ant.note: In a way that does not use much money or fuel.

people.definition: a lazy person who does nothing useful
people.example: His father called him a waster because he never studied.

context.text: My grandmother hates it when we waste bread. She says throwing food away is wasteful, so she makes soup from old bread.

reviewer_note: Split from the 'rubbish' row (separate map). wasted (adj) kept to the 'not useful' sense; informal slang 'drunk' omitted.

corpus_definition: Things that are not needed and are thrown away.

forms.definition: things that people throw away because they are not needed
forms.example: We should put our waste in the bin.

syn.note: British English, very common.
American English.
American English.
Formal, used by city services. Stress on the first part: REF-use.
Rubbish that people drop in the street or park.

forms.definition: to use money, time or things badly
forms.example: Don't waste water when you brush your teeth.
forms.note: Belongs to waste = use badly, not rubbish.

forms.definition: no longer needed and ready to be thrown away
forms.example: Put the waste paper in the blue box.
forms.note: Used only before a noun: waste paper, waste water.

syn.note: Not wanted any more.
Already used; not always thrown away.

forms.definition: using more money, time or things than you need
forms.example: Buying new clothes every week is wasteful.
forms.note: Belongs to waste = use badly, not rubbish.

forms.definition: in a way that uses more than you need
forms.example: They spend their money wastefully.
forms.note: Belongs to waste = use badly, not rubbish.

context.text: Our street in Chilonzor has new bins for plastic waste. Waste paper goes in the blue bin, and food goes in the green one.

reviewer_note: Split from the 'use badly' row; compounds like wastebasket and wasteland left for the Compounds branch.
